sections.title: The Problem: One Request, Five Log Files, Zero Correlation
sections.content:
A user clicks "Place Order" and the request touches the API gateway, order service, inventory service, payment service, and notification service.
- The order fails.
- Where?
- You open five Kibana dashboards and search by timestamp, hoping the same second range catches the right log line in each service.
- It doesn't, because clocks are skewed by 200ms across hosts.
- You spend 40 minutes correlating logs that a trace ID would have linked in one click.

Distributed tracing solves this by assigning a single **trace ID** at the entry point (typically the API gateway) and propagating it in HTTP headers to every downstream call.
- Each service also generates a **span ID** for its portion of the work.
- Spans are linked into a tree that shows the full call path — which services were called, in what order, how long each took, and where the failure occurred.

The mental model is simple: a **trace** is the entire journey of one user request across all services.
- A **span** is one unit of work within that trace — a service processing the request, a database query, an HTTP call to a downstream dependency.
- Spans have parent-child relationships: the order service's span is the parent; the inventory and payment spans are children.
- The result is a flame graph showing exactly where time was spent and where errors occurred.

The standard propagation header is **W3C Trace Context** (`traceparent` / `tracestate`), which has replaced the older Zipkin B3 format. Using W3C headers ensures interoperability across languages, frameworks, and observability vendors — your Java services and your Go services and your Python scripts all participate in the same trace.

An analogy: a trace ID is a **luggage tag stuck on your suitcase at check-in**.
- Every airport, every carousel, every transit hub scans the same tag — so you can trace the bag from origin to final destination without each airport maintaining its own numbering.
- Miss the initial tag and you're searching every carousel at every airport for a suitcase matching the description.

sections.title: Spring Boot 3 Auto-Instrumentation — Near-Zero Code Required
sections.content:
Spring Boot 3 integrated Micrometer Tracing as the native observability API, replacing the old Spring Cloud Sleuth library. The setup is two dependencies and three lines of YAML — most of the instrumentation happens automatically.

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId>
    <artifactId>micrometer-tracing-bridge-brave</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.zipkin.reporter2</groupId>
    <artifactId>zipkin-reporter-brave</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

```yaml
management:
  tracing:
    sampling:
      probability: 1.0         # 100% in dev; 0.05–0.10 in production
spring:
  application:
    name: order-service        # appears in trace metadata
logging:
  pattern:
    level: "%5p [${spring.application.name},%X{traceId},%X{spanId}]"
```

With this configuration, every log line automatically includes the trace and span IDs. When you search for `traceId=abc123` in your log aggregator, you get every log line from every service that participated in that request — in order.

The auto-instrumentation covers `RestTemplate`, `WebClient`, `RestClient`, Spring Data JPA, `@Async` methods, and scheduled tasks. Each outgoing HTTP call automatically injects the `traceparent` header; each incoming call extracts it. You don't write any propagation code. The only requirement is that you use Spring's HTTP clients instead of raw `java.net.HttpURLConnection` — Spring can only instrument what it controls.

sections.title: Custom Spans and Async Propagation — Where Auto-Instrumentation Falls Short
Sampling Strategy — The Cost vs Visibility Balance
sections.content:
Tracing 100% of requests in production is expensive. Each span generates metadata that must be collected, transmitted, stored, and indexed. At 10,000 RPS across 5 services with an average of 4 spans per request, that's 200,000 spans per second — roughly 50GB of storage per day in Zipkin or Jaeger.

The standard approach is **probability-based sampling** — trace a percentage of requests.
- Start at 5–10% for most services.
- This gives you enough traces for general latency analysis while keeping storage costs manageable.
- Keep the ability to **dynamically raise sampling** during incidents — a feature flag or config server change that bumps to 100% when you're actively debugging.

Even unsampled traces should have their IDs in log lines.
- The log pattern `%X{traceId}` works regardless of whether the trace is exported to Zipkin.
- This means you can always correlate logs by trace ID — you just won't have the visual flame graph in the trace UI.
- For the traces that are sampled, set a retention policy (7–14 days) to prevent storage from growing indefinitely.

Sampling can be smarter than random.
- **Error-biased sampling** always exports traces that contain an error span, regardless of the probability setting.
- This ensures you always have trace data for failures, which are the traces you actually need during incidents.
- Resilience4j and Micrometer support this through custom `Sampler` implementations that check the span's error state before deciding whether to export.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Trace = full journey, span = one unit of work** — trace ID ties all services together; parent-child relationships build a flame graph.
- **W3C `traceparent` header** — the interoperability standard; ensures Java, Go, Python, and Node services contribute to the same trace.
- **100% sampling melts storage** — 10K RPS × 5 services × 4 spans ≈ 50GB/day; use 5–10% with error-biased override.
- **Async boundaries silently break traces** — Kafka consumers and `@Async` lose context unless you inject/extract headers at boundaries.
- **Log correlation works without sampling** — `%X{traceId}` in log pattern adds trace IDs even for unsampled traces.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Distributed tracing solves the problem of debugging requests that span multiple services. When an order fails in production, you need to know exactly where it failed — the gateway, the order service, the inventory check, or the payment call. Without tracing, you're correlating five log files by timestamp and hoping server clocks are synchronized.

**How it works:**
- A trace ID is assigned at the entry point and propagated in W3C `traceparent` headers to every downstream call; each service generates a span ID for its work, with parent-child relationships building a flame graph
- In Spring Boot 3, Micrometer Tracing handles propagation automatically through `RestTemplate`, `WebClient`, and Spring Data without code changes; add the log pattern `%X{traceId}` to correlate logs across services with a single search

**The async boundary gotcha:**
- When the order service publishes to Kafka, the consumer loses trace context because there's no HTTP header to extract from the message
- You must explicitly inject the trace context into Kafka record headers at publish time, and extract it in the consumer; without this, the consumer's trace appears orphaned with no connection to the originating request

**Sampling strategy:**
- Never sample at 100% — at 10K RPS across 5 services, that's 50GB of trace data per day in Zipkin or Jaeger
- Use 5–10% probability sampling with error-biased override so failures are always captured regardless of the sampling rate; log correlation with `%X{traceId}` still works on unsampled requests

I recommend wiring Micrometer Tracing from day one — retrofitting trace propagation through async boundaries is significantly harder than getting it right at service creation time.

Spans are exported to **Zipkin** (or **Jaeger**/Tempo) for visualization. Each request gets a unique traceId that flows through every service in the call chain.

sections.title: When a User Reports a Slow Checkout, You Need One ID That Connects Logs Across Five Services — That's the Entire Point of Distributed Tracing
sections.content:
In a monolith, debugging a slow request means reading one thread's stack trace.
- In microservices, a single checkout fans out: API Gateway → Order Service → Inventory Service → Payment Service → Notification Service.
- Each service writes its own logs.
- When the user reports a 5-second delay, you know the request entered the gateway and eventually completed — but which service was slow?
- The Payment Service log shows a call took time, the Inventory log shows nothing unusual, and there's no way to connect them to the same user request without a shared identifier.

**Distributed tracing provides the connection: a trace ID generated at the entry point and propagated through every service in the call chain.** Each service records its work as a span — a named, timed unit — linked to the trace.
- The result is a tree of spans with exact timing: inventory check took 50ms, payment authorization took 4.8 seconds, notification took 10ms. The bottleneck is immediately visible.

The mistake many candidates make: conflating tracing with metrics.
- **Metrics are aggregated statistics** — 95th-percentile latency over the last 5 minutes, total request count per endpoint.
- Prometheus and Micrometer Meters answer: "Is the system behaving normally overall?
- **Tracing is per-request detail** — exactly what happened to this specific request, which services it touched, and how long each took.
- Zipkin and Jaeger answer: "What went wrong with request X?
- You need both; they are complementary tools, not alternatives.

Micrometer Tracing replaced Spring Cloud Sleuth in Spring Boot 3. The programming model is the same, but the library is now part of the Micrometer ecosystem rather than Spring Cloud.

sections.title: Setup — Two Dependencies and Zero Code Changes for Automatic HTTP Tracing
sections.content:
Micrometer Tracing auto-instruments Spring's HTTP stack — incoming requests, RestTemplate, WebClient, Feign, and Spring Cloud Stream messaging — without any annotations or code changes. Add the tracer bridge and a reporter, then configure the export endpoint.

```xml
<!-- Micrometer Tracing + Brave tracer bridge -->
<dependency>
  <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId>
  <artifactId>micrometer-tracing-bridge-brave</artifactId>
</dependency>
<!-- Zipkin span reporter -->
<dependency>
  <groupId>io.zipkin.reporter2</groupId>
  <artifactId>zipkin-reporter-brave</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

```yaml
management:
  tracing:
    sampling:
      probability: 0.1     # sample 10% of requests; 1.0 for dev/staging
  zipkin:
    tracing:
      endpoint: http://zipkin:9411/api/v2/spans
```

With these two changes, every HTTP request that arrives at your service gets a trace context. If a trace ID already exists in the incoming headers, the service creates a child span under that trace. If no trace ID is present, the service creates a new trace. Every outgoing HTTP call carries the current trace ID forward in the headers.

Micrometer also injects `traceId` and `spanId` into the **MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context)** automatically. Every log line your application writes includes these IDs without any changes to your logging code. This is the practical daily benefit developers notice first: searching a log aggregator by trace ID returns every log line across all services for that specific request.

sections.title: How Context Crosses Service Boundaries — HTTP Headers and Messaging Headers
sections.content:
Trace context propagation is the mechanism connecting spans across services. When Service A calls Service B, Micrometer injects the current trace and span IDs into HTTP headers before sending. Service B extracts them, creates a child span linked to Service A's span, and the trace tree grows.

Two header formats are in production use today:

- **B3 propagation** (Zipkin's original format): separate headers — `X-B3-TraceId`, `X-B3-SpanId`, `X-B3-ParentSpanId`, `X-B3-Sampled`. Compatible with older Zipkin deployments and many non-Spring services. The multi-header format is `B3_MULTI`; a single-header format (`b3: {traceId}-{spanId}-{sampling}`) is `B3_SINGLE`.
- **W3C TraceContext** (`traceparent` header): `traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01` — one header containing version, trace ID, parent span ID, and flags. The emerging standard, natively supported by OpenTelemetry and modern observability platforms.

Configure with `management.tracing.propagation.type=B3_MULTI` (Micrometer default) or `W3C`. In a polyglot environment, W3C is the better choice — it's supported by OpenTelemetry SDKs for Go, Node, Python, and others.

For **asynchronous messaging** via Spring Cloud Stream or Spring Kafka, Micrometer injects trace context into message headers automatically.
- The consumer extracts the context and creates a span linked to the producer's trace — connecting asynchronous flows across broker boundaries.
- A trace tree can span: HTTP request → Kafka producer → Kafka consumer → downstream HTTP call — all as a single unified trace, making it possible to debug end-to-end latency across synchronous and asynchronous boundaries.

sections.title: Sampling Strategies, Custom Business Spans, and the Log Search Pattern That Replaces Manual Correlation
How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
In microservices, a single request fans out across multiple services. Without distributed tracing, **correlating logs across services is impossible.** You see errors in isolation with no way to trace them back to the originating request.

Distributed tracing assigns a **trace ID** at the entry point and propagates it to every downstream service. Each service's work is a **span** with timing data. The full trace is a tree of spans.

Micrometer Tracing (replacing Sleuth in Boot 3) generates IDs and propagates context automatically via HTTP headers. Zipkin collects and visualizes the traces — its timeline view shows exactly which service is the bottleneck.

**Sampling is critical** — tracing 100% of requests in production generates enormous data. 10% sampling is common, but always force-trace errors.

The most practical benefit: trace ID in every log line via MDC. Search by trace ID to reconstruct the full request flow across all services.

In practice, I use Micrometer Tracing with Brave, Zipkin for visualization, and 10% sampling with 100% error tracing.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Trace ID propagates across all services via W3C traceparent header** — generated at the entry point; every downstream service includes it in logs and passes it forward; correlates the full request flow.
- **Micrometer Tracing replaced Spring Cloud Sleuth in Boot 3** — vendor-neutral abstraction supporting Brave and OpenTelemetry; auto-instruments RestTemplate, WebClient, and messaging.
- **Sampling 100% of requests in production is impractical** — 10% sampling (`management.tracing.sampling.probability=0.1`) balances observability with storage costs; force-trace errors regardless of sampling rate.
- **Trace ID injected into MDC enables log correlation** — every log line includes `traceId` and `spanId`; searching by trace ID across all service logs reconstructs the request flow.
- **Zipkin dependency graph shows service-to-service call patterns** — identifies which services are called most frequently and which spans have the highest latency; essential for finding bottlenecks.
